content:
Katara woke me before dawn and told me to dress warmly.

I had learned enough about her family to ask a better question.

“How warmly?”

She considered.

“Toph would call it oppressive.”

I put on another layer.

We left before anyone else woke.

Or rather, before anyone else admitted to being awake. As we closed the door, Toph’s voice came from the dark room behind us.

“If you get eaten by a seal, I’m not helping.”

Katara called back, “Go to sleep.”

“I am asleep.”

Aang made a muffled laughing noise.

Outside, the settlement was blue with early light.

Katara led me past the harbor, beyond the last cluster of new buildings, toward an open stretch of snow where wind had polished the surface hard.

She carried two waterskins and a small bundle of food.

I carried questions and kept them to myself.

Eventually we reached a flat basin surrounded by low ice ridges.

Katara stopped.

“This was where I practiced.”

I looked around.

“Waterbending?”

“Bad waterbending.”

“You were self-taught.”

“Mostly.”

She smiled at the memory.

“I used to come out here and try forms I’d invented from watching waves, or from old stories Gran Gran remembered. Half the time I froze my own boots to the ground.”

I tried to imagine Katara younger. Angry. Hopeful. Desperate for a teacher who did not exist.

“I wish I could have seen it.”

“No, you don’t.”

“I absolutely do.”

“I was terrible.”

“That’s why.”

She shoved me lightly.

Then she stepped onto the ice.

The change in her was immediate.

At home, Katara bent with efficiency. In the clinic, water became a tool of healing. In conflict, it became extension and defense and force.

Here she played.

A ribbon of water rose from beneath a thin cut in the ice. She spun it around her wrist, sent it arcing overhead, split it into dozens of droplets, froze them into glittering beads, then melted them before they landed.

“Show-off,” I said.

“Yes.”

The honesty made me laugh.

She bent a low wave across the ice toward my boots.

I jumped back.

It stopped an inch from me.

Katara grinned.

“I thought this was a meaningful childhood place.”

“It is.”

Another wave chased me.

I ran.

For ten minutes, Master Katara, hero of the Hundred Year War, one of the greatest waterbenders alive, used her art to harass a nonbender across a frozen field.

I lost badly.

Eventually I collapsed onto a snowbank, breathless.

Katara sat beside me.

Steam rose from her gloves where she warmed them with controlled bending.

“Can you do that for my feet?”

“No.”

“Cruel.”

“You should have worn the other socks.”

“You said these were enough.”

“I said those were enough with the lined boots.”

I stared at her.

She stared back.

“Toph is right about you.”

“Toph is never right about me.”

“Statistically impossible.”

Katara laughed and finally warmed the snow around my boots just enough to make the cold bearable.

We ate breakfast sitting on the ice.

For a while we talked about nothing important.

Then Katara said, “People think I’m warmer than I am.”

I looked at her.

She watched sunlight begin to edge over the horizon.

“I don’t mean kind. I think I’m kind.”

“You are.”

“I mean easy.”

The word settled.

I waited.

“They expect me to be easy to love because I take care of people.”

I thought about the clinic. The speeches. Her ability to find hope when everyone else had misplaced it.

“And then?”

“Then I’m stubborn. Or angry. Or I remember exactly what somebody said six months ago.”

“Terrifying skill.”

“Or I don’t forgive something.”

Her voice changed there.

I looked down at my mitten—the bad-fitting one Gran Gran had given me.

“Or you want things done your way.”

Katara gave me a look.

“I’m helping.”

“You are proving the point.”

“Also helping.”

She smiled despite herself.

Then the smile faded.

“I used to think love meant being needed.”

The confession caught me.

Katara rubbed one thumb over the seam of her glove.

“When Mom died, there was so much to do. Sokka needed me. The village needed everyone. Dad left to fight. Taking care of people felt like… if I was useful enough, maybe nobody else would disappear.”

I did not touch her immediately.

We had spoken about my own version of that wound.

Not the same history.

A familiar shape.

“What changed?”

“Aang.”

She smiled a little.

“Toph. Sokka growing up. Me getting tired.”

“Excellent teacher.”

“The worst.”

She exhaled.

“And you.”

I turned.

Katara’s eyes met mine.

“You let me do things for you.”

“That sounds like I’m failing the lesson.”

“No.” She nudged my knee. “You also say no.”

I understood.

Care that could be refused was different from care that created debt.

“You don’t need me every time I want to be needed,” she said. “I hate it.”

I laughed.

“But it’s good.”

The sun broke over the ridge.

Light scattered across the ice so brightly I had to narrow my eyes.

Katara watched me instead of the sunrise.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“That is never true.”

Her mouth curved.

“I love you.”

The words had been hovering around us for months in every practical gesture and furious argument.

Hearing them still changed the air.

I stopped breathing for a second.

Katara’s expression shifted.

Not panic.

Space.

She did not rush to fill my silence or demand the words back.

I reached for her hand.

“I love you too.”

The relief that crossed her face was so open it hurt.

She kissed me on the ice.

Not a first kiss.

Better.

A kiss that had history behind it.

Arguments. Missed lunch. Threats. Soup. Snow. Her hand on my back after meetings. My fingers at her wrist when anger needed somewhere precise to go.

When we pulled apart, my nose was cold enough to ache.

“Romantic,” I said.

Katara laughed against my cheek.

“Want to go back?”

“Yes.”

“Immediately?”

“My feet are becoming spiritual concepts.”

We stood.

Halfway home, Katara slipped her hand into mine.

The world around us was ice.

Nothing about it was empty.

Nothing about it was simple.

Ice preserved tracks. It carried weight. It cracked when pressure became too much. It melted and became water and froze again in another shape.

Katara squeezed my hand.

People mistook warmth for softness because they did not understand either.

Katara could be warm and sharp.

Tender and unforgiving.

A healer with anger in her bones.

Ice did not mean cold.

Sometimes it meant water had learned how to hold its ground.

The lesson Katara gave me on the ice had nothing to do with bending.

She showed me where to place my feet on packed snow, how to test a surface before trusting it, how to listen for the different sound ice made when water moved beneath it.

“You’re teaching me earthbender skills,” I said.

She looked offended. “This is Water Tribe survival.”

“Toph says standing your ground is hers.”

“Toph claims ownership of gravity when it benefits her.”

Fair.

We crossed a frozen inlet slowly. My muscles stayed tense until Katara stopped halfway and turned toward me.

“Look up.”

“I’m trying not to die.”

“You’re not going to die.”

“That confidence is suspicious.”

“Look up.”

I did.

The horizon had gone pink with sunrise. Ice caught the color in long fractured bands, every crack filled with light.

“Oh.”

Katara smiled.

“You can pay attention to danger without giving it everything.”

I glanced down again.

“Is that healer wisdom?”

“No. That’s me telling you to stop staring at your feet.”

We continued.

On the far bank she produced two cups from her pack and warmed tea with a spiral of water heated over a small flame we had carried in a covered brazier.

“Prepared,” I said.

“I travel with Aang. Preparation is survival.”

From somewhere behind us, very far away, Aang sneezed.

Katara laughed so hard she nearly spilled the tea.

Ice held beneath us. Not forever. Long enough.

On the way back, Katara showed me how to recognize snow beginning to crust over in wind and where fresh drifts could hide uneven ground. The lesson became practical again, which seemed to relax both of us.

“People romanticize the South,” she said.

“I was just romanticizing the sunrise.”

“That’s allowed.”

“Good.”

She glanced sideways. “The cold, less so.”

My toes had gone numb despite two pairs of socks. “I would never.”

Katara laughed and bent a ribbon of warmer water through a sealed skin before handing it to me.

“You planned that?”

“I know you.”

The words warmed more than the water did.

By the time the village roofs came back into view, I had learned three new ways not to fall through ice and one more way Katara loved: preparation so thorough it could masquerade as inevitability.

At the door, Katara knocked snow from my sleeves and said, “Next time, better boots.” I told her next time she was carrying me. She considered it far too seriously.
